subject: Chemistry
title: The Texas City Disaster of 1947
description: One-minute skill: The Texas City Disaster of 1947.

hook.text: In 1947, a ship loaded with 2,300 tons of ammonium nitrate exploded in Texas City, killing 581 people.

buildup.text: Ammonium nitrate is a common fertilizer. But when heated, it can decompose explosively—releasing massive gas volumes.

discovery.text: A fire broke out in the ship's hold. The crew tried to smother it, trapping heat inside and accelerating the reaction.

twist.text: The explosion was so powerful it created a 4.5-meter tidal wave. A second ship with more ammonium nitrate exploded 16 hours later.

climax.text: The disaster led to the first class-action lawsuit against the US government—and new fertilizer storage laws.

punchline.text: Fertilizer plus heat equals bomb. A common chemical turned catastrophic.

quiz.question: What caused the Texas City disaster of 1947?
options: Ammonium nitrate fertilizer overheated and detonated on a cargo ship
A natural gas pipeline under the port ruptured
Two oil tankers collided and ignited

details.summary: In 1947 the cargo ship Grandcamp, loaded with ammonium nitrate fertilizer, caught fire and detonated in Texas City harbor. The explosion killed nearly 600 people, triggered a chain reaction that detonated a second ship, and remains one of the deadliest industrial accidents in US history.
details.whyItMatters: Texas City demonstrated the catastrophic potential of ammonium nitrate in bulk quantities and led to the first major industrial disaster lawsuits in the United States.
takeaways: 2,300 tons of ammonium nitrate detonated aboard the Grandcamp
The explosion triggered fires and a second ship detonation hours later
It was the deadliest industrial disaster in US history at the time

faq.question: How did the fire on the Grandcamp start?
faq.answer: A small fire likely started from a discarded cigarette or spontaneous combustion in the hold. Crew members attempted to fight it with steam rather than water, which may have increased the temperature without extinguishing the flames, eventually triggering the ammonium nitrate detonation.

faq.question: Did the Texas City disaster lead to changes in safety regulations?
faq.answer: Yes. It prompted federal investigations and significant legal precedent through lawsuits against the US government for negligent handling of surplus war material. It accelerated industrial safety regulation and hazardous materials shipping protocols in the United States.
